justice: The narrow lane allocates almost all usable space to mixed vehicle movement, with no dedicated sidewalk or bike lane visible for different user groups.
Utility poles stand directly at the road edge and overhead cables crowd the corridor, indicating limited orderly space distribution for non-motorized users.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free edge treatments are visible, weakening accessibility for users with different mobility needs.
safety: Construction debris and loose rubble on the left side intrude into the walking edge and create tripping and collision hazards.
There is no visible sidewalk, curb separation, or protective buffer, so pedestrians would need to share the carriageway with cars and bikes.
The lane is lined with utility poles and dense overhead wires close to the roadway, while the long, enclosed walls reduce escape space and perceived security.
livability: The street appears quiet and low-traffic, which can support a calm residential atmosphere.
However, blank walls, gated facades, and limited visible storefronts or active frontages reduce street activity and everyday social vitality.
Debris piles, weathered building edges, and unmanaged roadside conditions weaken the sense of care and neighborhood amenity.
sustainability: The narrow street form and low-speed environment could support short local trips without heavy road infrastructure.
Vegetation is present along the right wall and with several trees, adding some green cover and ecological value.
But no visible bike facilities, permeable drainage features, stormwater infrastructure, or public transit elements are present, limiting broader sustainable mobility and environmental performance.
aesthetics: Mature trees and climbing greenery on the right side soften the corridor and improve visual texture.
At the same time, tangled overhead wires and numerous utility poles create strong visual clutter above the street.
Aging facades, blank walls, and visible rubble on the left side reduce overall visual quality and coherence.
comfort: Tree cover and vine-covered walls provide partial shade, but the street still has large exposed sunny areas that likely reduce thermal comfort in hot weather.
The absence of sidewalks, benches, or resting places lowers physical comfort for people moving along the lane.
Debris, uneven edge conditions, and close proximity to poles and walls can create psychological discomfort and make movement feel constrained.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, forcing walking directly in the vehicular lane.
Roadside rubble and clutter interrupt the usable edge space and make pedestrian passage less convenient.
There are no marked crossings, curb extensions, wayfinding elements, or pedestrian-priority features visible to support comfortable walking.
bikeability: There is no dedicated bike lane, pavement marking, or protective separation for cyclists.
The narrow carriageway, shared with motor vehicles and roadside obstacles, would create conflicts for bicycle travel.
Utility poles at the edge and debris near the roadside reduce lateral clearance and make cycling less forgiving and less comfortable.
